source.title: Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training
source.authors: Jing-Yan Shen; Ang Li; Salman Rahman; Yi-Fan Sun; Micah Goldblum; Matus Telgarsky; P. Izmailov

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to a controlled chess pretraining-to-RL pipeline and a math-domain language-model case study, reporting results on pretraining loss, compute allocation, and downstream performance.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports policy-evolution and reasoning-trace results, but those do not measure the scaling-law claims here. Its comparisons of SFT variants and policy diagnostics are not included as rows unless they directly report a downstream-predictability result.
record.test_reason: The study refits the Chinchilla loss form to a new pretraining domain: chess move sequences, 5M–1B parameters, compute 6.5e16–6.5e19 FLOPs. From that fit it derives compute-optimal N/D exponents and compares them with Hoffmann et al. It also measures how post-SFT and post-RL downstream pass@k track pretraining loss and tokens, in chess and in a 1B math-text OLMo-2 case. These are its own results on V1, V3, V5, V6 and V7 in a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that pretraining loss predicts post-RL pass@1 and that pretraining data scale predicts the local RL improvement rate. They find the optimal RL share grows with total compute, and that RL helps pass@1 more than pass@16. For pretraining, the chess loss follows the Chinchilla form with a similar α but a much steeper β, favouring more tokens per parameter. They call the math result early qualitative evidence of transfer and caution against extrapolating beyond 1B.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a controlled chess pretraining/SFT/RL pipeline and fits a Chinchilla-style loss form plus a joint pretraining–RL reward law; it is not a reproduction of the original language-model scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured RL-slope relationship depends on benchmark difficulty and saturation; reference-compute choice changes the fitted reference reward relationship; the paper compares alternative functional forms and notes that slope fitting is local to the observed RL range.

fits_no_version.finding: Compute-optimal RL share along the pretraining+RL frontier rises from about 20% (50M) to about 28% (680M).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In chess, the compute-optimal RL fraction increases with total compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-RL pass@1 is approximately linear in log10 RL compute, as a local approximation of a sigmoid. Pretraining tokens set the slope.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Local RL reward is log-linear in RL compute, with a slope set mainly by pretraining data scale.

record.problems: The main scaling sweeps are in chess, with models up to 1B parameters; the math transfer test uses one fixed-architecture model family. The RL law is explicitly a local approximation, its slope component is noisier than the reference-reward component, and the authors caution against extrapolation beyond the observed range. Some plotted fits are reported graphically.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported scaling results were omitted.

untested.parts: Natural-language pretraining loss; models beyond 1B; separate one-variable power laws in N, D or C with the others non-limiting.
Entire version. No pretraining-loss prediction for runs orders of magnitude larger; held-out tests predict downstream reward within or near the observed size range.
Stability of the allocation exponents beyond 6.5e19 FLOPs. Natural-language allocation. No independent IsoFLOP-derived exponent is reported.
Entire version. Architectures are fixed deep designs; there is no shape comparison at fixed N.
Image/video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer scaling laws. Only the chess-sequence pretraining loss is tested.
Parameter-counting, schedule or fitting-method comparisons for the loss law.

missing.what: Out-of-sample sizes 32M and 410M: Chinchilla-L RMSE 0.0232 overall, 410M up to 0.037
IsoFLOP optima: chess favours smaller models and more tokens than D/N=20, converging at higher compute; pass@1/16 optima track the loss optimum
Math GSM8K and MATH500 loss/slope fits (GSM8K slope quad R² 0.58; MATH500 slope R² 0.90)
RL asymptote ceiling vs pretraining loss for the 20M family (Spearman −0.73, R² 0.90)
Post-SFT R0 vs loss on B3–B4: exponential R² 0.70, linear 0.51; B2 slope weakly predicted by loss
Post-RL optimal pretraining tokens show no systematic deviation from the chess Chinchilla allocation

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this study. V2 is not tested: all held-out prediction concerns downstream reward within or near the 20M–680M range, so the reader's V2 labels are removed. R12 and R13 are re-linked from V5 to V6, because math-domain text is text pretraining. V5 support rests on the chess-sequence loss fit instead. The record's V1 limits_scope (exponent differs) belongs under V7 and is dropped. The V6 label on R11 was flagged because R11 was not linked to V6; R11 is now linked to V6. Rows R14–R19 are unchanged.

versions.untested_parts: Tests a Chinchilla-style loss fit on chess models, not held-out natural-language pretraining loss across several orders of magnitude.
Tests leave-one-out and leave-one-model-size-out prediction within the observed runs; it does not establish prediction for runs orders of magnitude larger.
Tests compute-optimal parameter/token exponents in chess, not whether the same exponents apply to large-scale language-model training.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Tests a math-text case study only; does not test image/video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes broadly.
Tests chess and math downstream pass@k/pass@1 relationships; does not establish predictability across general downstream tasks.
Tests sensitivity to benchmark saturation and some fitting choices, but does not systematically compare data mixtures or training schedules.
